prompts.text: What hobby did you pick up as a child because another family member enjoyed it?
Tell me about the first time you became completely absorbed in making something.
We set up a family afternoon to revisit old childhood hobbies. What materials should we collect?
Bring back an old drawing habit or try the musical instrument you once wanted to learn?
Children sometimes spend weeks fascinated by something adults barely notice.
An abandoned childhood hobby still teaches us something about what we used to enjoy.
Which childhood interest surprised your family because nobody else shared it?
Describe a project you started as a child and never quite finished.
A younger relative wants to try a hobby you once loved. What's the first thing you'd show them?
What activity did you think you'd grow up doing professionally when you were small?
What family outing felt like a major expedition when you were young?
Tell me about a journey where the conversations in the vehicle became the main entertainment.
We recreate a childhood family outing with one afternoon available. Which stop should we keep?
Visit a childhood picnic spot or revisit a place where the family used to shop together?
Children often remember the snacks and songs from a journey more clearly than the destination.
A short outing with plenty of surprises can leave a bigger childhood memory than a long holiday.
Who in the family always remembered to pack the things everyone else forgot?
Describe the first time you travelled somewhere without a parent beside you.
A younger relative asks what travelling was like before map apps. What family story would you share?
What journey from childhood would you like to retrace as an adult?
What's the strangest thing you tried to build using whatever you found at home?
Tell me about a childhood experiment that produced an unexpected result.
We give the children cardboard, string and tape for an afternoon. What challenge should they attempt?
Build a miniature town from boxes or invent a new board game with handmade pieces?
A child's improvised invention sometimes solves a problem adults have stopped noticing.
The most useful part of a childhood experiment is often the question it creates.
Did you ever take something apart because you wanted to know how it worked?
Describe an invention you proudly presented to your family, even if it barely worked.
A young cousin asks us to help design a simple paper bridge. What would you let them try first?
What everyday household object seemed mysterious to you when you were little?
Which family joke makes more sense when someone explains where it started?
Tell me about a childhood misunderstanding that still makes the family laugh.
We're making a light-hearted family quiz about growing up. What question should everyone attempt?
Retell a funny family story or act out a harmless moment from an old gathering?
The same family story often gets a little funnier each time a different person tells it.
A running family joke is worth keeping only while the person at its centre enjoys it.
Who in the family had the best way of making children laugh without telling a joke?
Describe an ordinary childhood moment that became unexpectedly funny.
Two relatives claim to have invented the same family catchphrase. How do we settle the debate?
What's a childhood phrase our family used that outsiders would find confusing?
What was the first household task you felt genuinely proud to handle on your own?
Tell me about a time an older relative trusted you with a small responsibility.
We want to teach younger family members a practical task. How do we make it interesting rather than a chore?
Learn to organise a family meal or learn how to care for a small garden?
A task that seems simple to an adult can feel like a milestone to a child.
Children often grow more confident when adults explain why a job matters.
Which childhood chore do you still do the same way you were taught?
Describe a mistake you made while learning a task and the useful lesson it left you.
A younger cousin wants to help prepare for visitors. Which job would you offer them?
What family responsibility taught you the most about working with other people?
What programme did you rush home to watch when you were younger?
Tell me about a family evening when everyone gathered around the same television or radio.
We organise a retro entertainment night for the family. What should appear on the programme?
Listen to old radio stories together or watch an episode of a childhood television favourite?
Waiting for a programme to air gave families a different kind of shared anticipation.
Some childhood shows are more enjoyable to remember than to rewatch.
What advert or theme tune from childhood do you still remember without trying?
Describe an entertainer who made a lasting impression on you when you were young.
A younger relative asks why people used to plan their evenings around television schedules. How would you explain it?
Which childhood programme would you enjoy showing someone who has never heard of it?
What question did you ask adults repeatedly because their answers never quite satisfied you?
Tell me about a childhood question that led to a surprisingly interesting family discussion.
A child asks why people in our family speak more than one language. Where would you begin?
Answer a child's question with a demonstration or find a book to read together?
Children sometimes notice contradictions that adults have learned to ignore.
A thoughtful 'I don't know' is better than an answer an adult has made up on the spot.
What's something you misunderstood as a child because nobody explained the full story?
Describe an adult who took one of your childhood questions seriously.
A younger relative asks why two generations remember the same event differently. How might we discuss it?
What would you ask your younger self about the things they were curious about?
What device from your childhood would a younger family member struggle to operate?
Tell me about the first piece of technology in our home that seemed extraordinary at the time.
We set up a family demonstration of old household gadgets. Which one should be first?
Show everyone how a cassette player works or explain how photographs were developed on film?
New technology changes family routines long before people notice the change.
Older household devices deserve an explanation of how people used them, not only a display behind glass.
What task did your family do by hand when you were little that now takes a few taps?
Describe learning to use a new device from a younger or older relative.
Someone finds an old landline telephone. How would you explain the experience of sharing one family phone?
Which childhood technology do you miss for reasons other than nostalgia?
What childhood freedom did older relatives enjoy that feels unusual to younger people now?
Tell me about a conversation where two generations realised they shared the same childhood worry.
Three generations of our family answer one question about growing up. Which question would produce the best discussion?
Compare childhood school bags or compare the games each generation played after school?
A childhood experience can be common in one generation and unfamiliar in the next.
Comparing generations works best when everyone explains their circumstances rather than defends their choices.
What part of your childhood would you want younger relatives to understand without copying exactly?
Describe a time an older relative was surprised by how similar your childhood experience was to theirs.
We're recording a family history conversation. How do we make sure quieter relatives get a chance to contribute?
What is one childhood experience you hope future family members will have in their own way?
What season of the year felt most different when you were growing up?
Tell me about a childhood afternoon when the weather changed everyone's plans.
We recreate a favourite rainy-day activity for a family gathering. What should we prepare?
An early morning walk during the holidays or a cool evening playing outside?
Children often remember the weather around an important day as part of the story.
A family tradition doesn't need a special date if everyone enjoys doing it together.
What sounds outside the house told you it was time to go indoors?
Describe a childhood activity you only did during a particular season.
A younger relative asks what holidays felt like before everyone had personal devices. Which outdoor memory would you share?
Which seasonal family routine would you most enjoy bringing back?
